statement: A card has seven sentences on it, numbered 1 to 7. Sentence number k says: 'At most k of the sentences on this card are true.' How many of the seven sentences are true?

choices.misconception: I noticed that sentence 7 must be true and assumed that all seven sentences are therefore true.
I worked out that sentences 1, 2 and 3 are false and gave the number of false sentences instead of true ones.
I decided only sentence 7, the weakest claim, is true, without checking that this would make sentence 1 true as well.
I thought sentences that talk about themselves can never be true, so I said none of them are.

hints: Suppose exactly T sentences are true. Which sentences does that make true?
Assume a value and look for a contradiction. If exactly T sentences are true, work out which numbered sentences that makes true, count them, and see whether the count comes back to T.
If exactly T are true, sentence k is true exactly when k is T or more. That is sentences T to 7, which is 8 - T sentences. Set 8 - T equal to T.

solutions.reliable: Suppose exactly T sentences are true. Sentence k is true exactly when T is at most k, so the true sentences are numbers T, T + 1, ..., 7, and there are 8 - T of them. For the card to be consistent, 8 - T = T, so T = 4: sentences 4 to 7 are true and sentences 1 to 3 are false. Every other value contradicts itself; for example, if all 7 were true, sentence 1 would be claiming that at most one sentence is true. The transferable idea: assume a value, follow its consequences, and keep only the value that does not contradict itself.
solutions.elegant: Sentence 7 is certainly true, and if sentence k is true so is every later one. So the true sentences form a block ending at 7, and the block must start at its own length. A block from T to 7 has 8 - T members, and only the block 4, 5, 6, 7 starts at its length.

whyOnTest: Self-referring sentences are settled by assuming a count and hunting for a contradiction, which is the core move of informal proof.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
